Student Debt and the Class of 2020. 16th Annual Report
Schak, J. Oliver; Wong, Nancy; Fung, Ana
Project on Student Debt
"Student Debt and the Class of 2020" is The Institute for College Access & Success' (TICAS') sixteenth annual report on the student loan debt of recent graduates from four-year colleges, documenting changes and variation in student debt across states and colleges. State averages for debt at graduation in 2020 ranged from $18,350 (Utah) to $39,950 (New Hampshire), and new graduates' likelihood of having debt varied from 39 percent (Utah) to 73 percent (South Dakota). In 19 states, average debt was more than $30,000, and it was over $35,000 in six states. Many of the same states appear at the high and low ends of the spectrum as in previous years. High-debt states remain concentrated in the Northeast and low-debt states are mainly in the West. Available data on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on current students and borrowers suggest a cause for concern about college affordability and unaffordable debt burdens. This report includes federal policy recommendations to reduce debt burdens and manage repayment in the wake of COVID-19 and beyond. [For "Student Debt and the Class of 2019. 15th Annual Report," see ED609297.]

*   Delaware saw the largest total federal loan balance growth over five (5) years (**21.7%**).

"Student Debt and the Class of 2020" is The Institute for College Access & Success' (TICAS') sixteenth annual report on the student loan debt of recent graduates from four-year colleges, documenting changes and variation in student debt across states and colleges. State averages for debt at graduation in 2020 ranged from $18,350 (Utah) to $39,950 (New Hampshire), and new graduates' likelihood of having debt varied from 39 percent (Utah) to 73 percent (South Dakota). In 19 states, average debt was more than $30,000, and it was over $35,000 in six states. Many of the same states appear at the high and low ends of the spectrum as in previous years. High-debt states remain concentrated in the Northeast and low-debt states are mainly in the West. Available data on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on current students and borrowers suggest a cause for concern about college affordability and unaffordable debt burdens. This report includes federal policy recommendations to reduce debt burdens and manage repayment in the wake of COVID-19 and beyond. [For "Student Debt and the Class of 2019. 15th Annual Report," see ED609297.]

**Report Highlights.** District of Columbia residents have the nation’s highest average federal student loan debt at **$55,846** per borrower.
*   D.C. residents are also the most likely to have federal student loan debt; borrowers represent **20.1%** of adults.  
*   Californians have the largest collective federal student loan debt (**$156.7 billion**), and they represent the largest number of borrowers (_3.92 million_).  
*   Among states*, Hawaii saw the largest average federal student loan balance growth between 2021 and 2026 (**10.7%**).  
*   Delaware saw the largest total federal loan balance growth over five (5) years (**21.7%**).
*_The territory of Puerto Rico saw growth of the average balance and the total balance among federal student loan borrowers (25.8% and 30.0% respectively)._

## Student Loan Debt by State
Debt variations by location may be due to socioeconomic factors, such as a higher concentration of professionals with advanced degrees (e.g. health specialists with medical school debt) and as well as local accessibility of advanced education. Note that all student loan debt on this page refers to federal student loan debt only; private student loans are not a factor.
*   Texas saw the greatest borrower growth between 2021 and 2026, up by 12.0% (423,600 more with federal student loan debt).  
*   In every state, at least 62% of borrowers owe $40,000 or less.  
*   Among states, Wyoming has the largest share of borrowers with a federal student loan balance of $10,000 or less (36.9%).

## Student Loan Debt in Alabama
Federal student loan borrowers in Alabama owe an average of $39,157.
*   664,000 Alabama residents have federal student loan debt.  
*   Between 2021 and 2026, the average federal student loan balance among Alabama borrowers increased 4.84%.  
*   The average federal student loan balance in Alabama is 1.20% below the national average.  
*   Collectively, Alabama borrowers have a federal student loan debt balance of $26.00 billion.  
*   16.3% of adults in Alabama have federal student loan debt.  
*   Over five (5) years, the total federal student loan balance among Alabama borrowers increased $2.90 billion (12.55%); the number of borrowers grew by 45,500 (7.36%).  
*   70.6% of Alabama federal student loan borrowers owe $40,000 or less; their share represents 26.4% of the state’s total outstanding balance.  
*   30.1% of federal student loan borrowers in Alabama owe $10,000 or less.

*   The average federal student loan balance in Alaska is 6.12% below the national average.  
*   Collectively, Alaska borrowers have a federal student loan debt balance of $2.40 billion.  
*   11.4% of adults in Alaska have federal student loan debt.  
*   Over five (5) years, the total federal student loan balance among Alaska borrowers increased by $100 million (4.35%); the number of borrowers declined by 2,300 (3.44%).  
*   73.5% of Alaska federal student loan borrowers owe $40,000 or less; their share represents 28.0% of the state’s total outstanding balance.  
*   33.3% of federal student loan borrowers in Alaska owe $10,000 or less.

Title: Student Loan Debt by State [2026]: Average + Total Debt
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8
**Report Highlights.** District of Columbia residents have the nation’s highest average federal student loan debt at **$55,846** per borrower.
*   D.C. residents are also the most likely to have federal student loan debt; borrowers represent **20.1%** of adults.  
*   Californians have the largest collective federal student loan debt (**$156.7 billion**), and they represent the largest number of borrowers (_3.92 million_).  
*   Among states*, Hawaii saw the largest average federal student loan balance growth between 2021 and 2026 (**10.7%**).  
*   Delaware saw the largest total federal loan balance growth over five (5) years (**21.7%**).
*_The territory of Puerto Rico saw growth of the average balance and the total balance among federal student loan borrowers (25.8% and 30.0% respectively)._

## Student Loan Debt by State
Debt variations by location may be due to socioeconomic factors, such as a higher concentration of professionals with advanced degrees (e.g. health specialists with medical school debt) and as well as local accessibility of advanced education. Note that all student loan debt on this page refers to federal student loan debt only; private student loans are not a factor.
*   Texas saw the greatest borrower growth between 2021 and 2026, up by 12.0% (423,600 more with federal student loan debt).  
*   In every state, at least 62% of borrowers owe $40,000 or less.  
*   Among states, Wyoming has the largest share of borrowers with a federal student loan balance of $10,000 or less (36.9%).

Federal student loan borrowers in Alabama owe an average of $39,157.

*   The average federal student loan balance in Alabama is 1.20% below the national average.

*   16.3% of adults in Alabama have federal student loan debt.  
*   Over five (5) years, the total federal student loan balance among Alabama borrowers increased $2.90 billion (12.55%); the number of borrowers grew by 45,500 (7.36%).  
*   70.6% of Alabama federal student loan borrowers owe $40,000 or less; their share represents 26.4% of the state’s total outstanding balance.  
*   30.1% of federal student loan borrowers in Alabama owe $10,000 or less.

Student Debt and the Class of 2020. 16th Annual Report
Schak, J. Oliver; Wong, Nancy; Fung, Ana
Project on Student Debt
"Student Debt and the Class of 2020" is The Institute for College Access & Success' (TICAS') sixteenth annual report on the student loan debt of recent graduates from four-year colleges, documenting changes and variation in student debt across states and colleges. State averages for debt at graduation in 2020 ranged from $18,350 (Utah) to $39,950 (New Hampshire), and new graduates' likelihood of having debt varied from 39 percent (Utah) to 73 percent (South Dakota). In 19 states, average debt was more than $30,000, and it was over $35,000 in six states. Many of the same states appear at the high and low ends of the spectrum as in previous years. High-debt states remain concentrated in the Northeast and low-debt states are mainly in the West. Available data on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on current students and borrowers suggest a cause for concern about college affordability and unaffordable debt burdens. This report includes federal policy recommendations to reduce debt burdens and manage repayment in the wake of COVID-19 and beyond. [For "Student Debt and the Class of 2019. 15th Annual Report," see ED609297.]

Title: New Report Details Student Loan Debt Levels Across the Country
Chunks: 0,1,2
[By Owen Daugherty, NASFAA Staff Reporter](mailto:news@nasfaa.org)  
The student loan debt landscape is disparate and varied, and no one figure or data point can tell the full story of how Americans with bachelor’s degrees are faring with their student loan debt once they graduate.
In an attempt to paint a picture of the state of student loan debt in the country, the Institute for College Access and Success (TICAS) released its sixteenth annual report detailing the average debt for the class of 2020.
While the report does not include national figures for the average debt among graduates with bachelor’s degrees from public and nonprofit institutions, it does find vast variation in debt levels across states as well as colleges.
National figures were not included in this iteration of TICAS’ annual report because data from a nationally representative federal study that is typically released every four years by the Department of Education (ED), which will cover students who graduated in the class of 2020, is not slated to be released this year.
In recent years, TICAS noted the average amount of student debt that bachelor's degree graduates took on has remained steady and even decreased slightly in some years, though those flattening levels came amid all-time highs.
After increasing at an average of 4% per year from 1996 to 2012, the average debt level among all bachelor’s degree recipients from public and nonprofit institutions plateaued in 2016 at $29,650. From 2016 to 2019, average debt levels remained essentially flat.
"Despite flattening levels of student loan debt in recent years, the debt of graduating classes has remained near an all-time high, and the debt borrowers hold continues to make their lives financially perilous," TICAS president Sameer Gadkaree said in a statement accompanying the report. "Given pre-existing economic disparities and vast racial disparities in wealth accumulation in our country, the students who suffer most from these disruptions tend to be [​​Black, Indigenous, and People of Color], first-generation, and those from low-income backgrounds."

At the state level, average student debt upon graduation varied greatly, from the low of $18,350 in Utah to $39,950 at the high end in New Hampshire. Further, new graduates' likelihood of having debt varied from 39% in Utah to 73% in South Dakota, and in nineteen states, average debt was more than $30,000 and more than $35,000 in six states.
As for private debt, there was significant overlap among states with high average overall debt amounts and higher average private debt. Eight states were in the top 10 for both average private and overall debt, which includes federal, private, state, and institutional debt. Generally speaking, states with more private loan borrowing and high average private debt levels were concentrated in the Northeast, and states with less private debt were concentrated in the West.
It’s also instructive to analyze student loan debt loans by different types of loans, including federal and private student loans. On average, students who attended nonprofit institutions were more likely to graduate with debt from private loans and leave school with higher debt amounts compared to those who attend public institutions.
The share of graduates with private debt exceeded 15% at nearly 40% of nonprofit institutions, compared to 22% at public institutions, while the average private debt borrowed exceeded $50,000 at 15% of nonprofit institutions assessed in the report, compared to less than 1% at public institutions.
Overall, TICAS noted that recent surveys show that private student debt reached an all-time high at the onset of the coronavirus pandemic. The estimated total of private student debt among current and repaying students was at $136.3 billion in March 2021, a 47%increase from $92.6 billion in March 2014, the earliest year the data was reported. Private loans now make up nearly 8% of all student loan debt, TICAS added, and the origination of new private loans nearly doubled from academic year 2010-11 to 2018-19.
“Time will tell how the pandemic impacts the longer-term trends in private debt and its consequences for borrowers,” the report stated.

As relief measures enacted to provide relief to borrowers amid the pandemic are set to expire in the coming months, the report urges policymakers to consider the student loan debt many hold and ensure borrowers are protected. With tens of millions of borrowers set to resume payments when the pause on payments and interest accrual comes to an end Jan. 31, 2022, ED “must make a robust plan to ensure borrowers will be protected during this transition, especially as this transition coincides with major shifts in the servicing system.”
“Throughout the remainder of the pause, [ED] must provide borrowers with clear and actionable information and resources, including access to timely and accurate assistance and guidance from servicers and the Department,” the report stated.
To that end, ED is in the process of implementing measures to ensure borrowers have a smooth transition to repayment, as well as creating a safety net for borrowers who were in default on their loans before the pandemic, according to_Politico’s_ Michael Stratford.
Additionally, the report argues the department should clear the backlogs of claims related to borrower defense, total and permanent disability (TPD), and public service loan forgiveness (PSLF), something ED has already begun doing for borrowers with TPD and PSLF claims.
Other recommendations for federal policymakers included sustainable funding for public institutions, increasing need-based aid such as the federal Pell Grant, implementing better protections for borrowers with private loans, strengthening accountability mechanisms for institutions, and improving transparency and oversight.
As for long-term solutions that could alleviate the student debt many borrowers hold, the report recommends reforming the student loan payment system holistically.
“Policymakers should create an improved income-driven repayment plan that is easy to access, ensures more affordable monthly payments, prevents ballooning balances, and guarantees automatic, tax free forgiveness after a reasonable number of payments,” the report urges. “Policymakers must also reform the student loan default and collections system to give borrowers a fresh start.”

[By Owen Daugherty, NASFAA Staff Reporter](mailto:news@nasfaa.org)  
The student loan debt landscape is disparate and varied, and no one figure or data point can tell the full story of how Americans with bachelor’s degrees are faring with their student loan debt once they graduate.
In an attempt to paint a picture of the state of student loan debt in the country, the Institute for College Access and Success (TICAS) released its sixteenth annual report detailing the average debt for the class of 2020.
While the report does not include national figures for the average debt among graduates with bachelor’s degrees from public and nonprofit institutions, it does find vast variation in debt levels across states as well as colleges.
National figures were not included in this iteration of TICAS’ annual report because data from a nationally representative federal study that is typically released every four years by the Department of Education (ED), which will cover students who graduated in the class of 2020, is not slated to be released this year.
In recent years, TICAS noted the average amount of student debt that bachelor's degree graduates took on has remained steady and even decreased slightly in some years, though those flattening levels came amid all-time highs.
After increasing at an average of 4% per year from 1996 to 2012, the average debt level among all bachelor’s degree recipients from public and nonprofit institutions plateaued in 2016 at $29,650. From 2016 to 2019, average debt levels remained essentially flat.
"Despite flattening levels of student loan debt in recent years, the debt of graduating classes has remained near an all-time high, and the debt borrowers hold continues to make their lives financially perilous," TICAS president Sameer Gadkaree said in a statement accompanying the report. "Given pre-existing economic disparities and vast racial disparities in wealth accumulation in our country, the students who suffer most from these disruptions tend to be [​​Black, Indigenous, and People of Color], first-generation, and those from low-income backgrounds."

"Student Debt and the Class of 2020" is The Institute for College Access & Success' (TICAS') sixteenth annual report on the student loan debt of recent graduates from four-year colleges, documenting changes and variation in student debt across states and colleges. State averages for debt at graduation in 2020 ranged from $18,350 (Utah) to $39,950 (New Hampshire), and new graduates' likelihood of having debt varied from 39 percent (Utah) to 73 percent (South Dakota). In 19 states, average debt was more than $30,000, and it was over $35,000 in six states. Many of the same states appear at the high and low ends of the spectrum as in previous years. High-debt states remain concentrated in the Northeast and low-debt states are mainly in the West. Available data on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on current students and borrowers suggest a cause for concern about college affordability and unaffordable debt burdens. This report includes federal policy recommendations to reduce debt burdens and manage repayment in the wake of COVID-19 and beyond. Title: New Report Details Student Loan Debt Levels Across the Country
Chunks: 0,1,2
[By Owen Daugherty, NASFAA Staff Reporter](mailto:news@nasfaa.org)  
The student loan debt landscape is disparate and varied, and no one figure or data point can tell the full story of how Americans with bachelor’s degrees are faring with their student loan debt once they graduate.
In an attempt to paint a picture of the state of student loan debt in the country, the Institute for College Access and Success (TICAS) released its sixteenth annual report detailing the average debt for the class of 2020.
While the report does not include national figures for the average debt among graduates with bachelor’s degrees from public and nonprofit institutions, it does find vast variation in debt levels across states as well as colleges.
National figures were not included in this iteration of TICAS’ annual report because data from a nationally representative federal study that is typically released every four years by the Department of Education (ED), which will cover students who graduated in the class of 2020, is not slated to be released this year.
In recent years, TICAS noted the average amount of student debt that bachelor's degree graduates took on has remained steady and even decreased slightly in some years, though those flattening levels came amid all-time highs.
After increasing at an average of 4% per year from 1996 to 2012, the average debt level among all bachelor’s degree recipients from public and nonprofit institutions plateaued in 2016 at $29,650. From 2016 to 2019, average debt levels remained essentially flat.
"Despite flattening levels of student loan debt in recent years, the debt of graduating classes has remained near an all-time high, and the debt borrowers hold continues to make their lives financially perilous," TICAS president Sameer Gadkaree said in a statement accompanying the report. "Given pre-existing economic disparities and vast racial disparities in wealth accumulation in our country, the students who suffer most from these disruptions tend to be [​​Black, Indigenous, and People of Color], first-generation, and those from low-income backgrounds."

At the state level, average student debt upon graduation varied greatly, from the low of $18,350 in Utah to $39,950 at the high end in New Hampshire. Further, new graduates' likelihood of having debt varied from 39% in Utah to 73% in South Dakota, and in nineteen states, average debt was more than $30,000 and more than $35,000 in six states.
As for private debt, there was significant overlap among states with high average overall debt amounts and higher average private debt. Eight states were in the top 10 for both average private and overall debt, which includes federal, private, state, and institutional debt. Generally speaking, states with more private loan borrowing and high average private debt levels were concentrated in the Northeast, and states with less private debt were concentrated in the West.
It’s also instructive to analyze student loan debt loans by different types of loans, including federal and private student loans. On average, students who attended nonprofit institutions were more likely to graduate with debt from private loans and leave school with higher debt amounts compared to those who attend public institutions.
The share of graduates with private debt exceeded 15% at nearly 40% of nonprofit institutions, compared to 22% at public institutions, while the average private debt borrowed exceeded $50,000 at 15% of nonprofit institutions assessed in the report, compared to less than 1% at public institutions.
Overall, TICAS noted that recent surveys show that private student debt reached an all-time high at the onset of the coronavirus pandemic. The estimated total of private student debt among current and repaying students was at $136.3 billion in March 2021, a 47%increase from $92.6 billion in March 2014, the earliest year the data was reported. Private loans now make up nearly 8% of all student loan debt, TICAS added, and the origination of new private loans nearly doubled from academic year 2010-11 to 2018-19.
“Time will tell how the pandemic impacts the longer-term trends in private debt and its consequences for borrowers,” the report stated.

As relief measures enacted to provide relief to borrowers amid the pandemic are set to expire in the coming months, the report urges policymakers to consider the student loan debt many hold and ensure borrowers are protected. With tens of millions of borrowers set to resume payments when the pause on payments and interest accrual comes to an end Jan. 31, 2022, ED “must make a robust plan to ensure borrowers will be protected during this transition, especially as this transition coincides with major shifts in the servicing system.”
“Throughout the remainder of the pause, [ED] must provide borrowers with clear and actionable information and resources, including access to timely and accurate assistance and guidance from servicers and the Department,” the report stated.
To that end, ED is in the process of implementing measures to ensure borrowers have a smooth transition to repayment, as well as creating a safety net for borrowers who were in default on their loans before the pandemic, according to_Politico’s_ Michael Stratford.
Additionally, the report argues the department should clear the backlogs of claims related to borrower defense, total and permanent disability (TPD), and public service loan forgiveness (PSLF), something ED has already begun doing for borrowers with TPD and PSLF claims.
Other recommendations for federal policymakers included sustainable funding for public institutions, increasing need-based aid such as the federal Pell Grant, implementing better protections for borrowers with private loans, strengthening accountability mechanisms for institutions, and improving transparency and oversight.
As for long-term solutions that could alleviate the student debt many borrowers hold, the report recommends reforming the student loan payment system holistically.
“Policymakers should create an improved income-driven repayment plan that is easy to access, ensures more affordable monthly payments, prevents ballooning balances, and guarantees automatic, tax free forgiveness after a reasonable number of payments,” the report urges. “Policymakers must also reform the student loan default and collections system to give borrowers a fresh start.”

Schak, J. Oliver; Wong, Nancy; Fung, Ana
Project on Student Debt
"Student Debt and the Class of 2020" is The Institute for College Access & Success' (TICAS') sixteenth annual report on the student loan debt of recent graduates from four-year colleges, documenting changes and variation in student debt across states and colleges. State averages for debt at graduation in 2020 ranged from $18,350 (Utah) to $39,950 (New Hampshire), and new graduates' likelihood of having debt varied from 39 percent (Utah) to 73 percent (South Dakota). In 19 states, average debt was more than $30,000, and it was over $35,000 in six states. Many of the same states appear at the high and low ends of the spectrum as in previous years. High-debt states remain concentrated in the Northeast and low-debt states are mainly in the West. Available data on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on current students and borrowers suggest a cause for concern about college affordability and unaffordable debt burdens. This report includes federal policy recommendations to reduce debt burdens and manage repayment in the wake of COVID-19 and beyond. steps.text:
**Step 1 –  High‑debt states (TICAS, *Student Debt and the Class of 2020*)**  
The TICAS report makes it clear that the “high‑debt” group is concentrated in the Northeast.  The report’s state‑by‑state table (see § 11 of the PDF) shows that **eight of the ten states with the highest average debt per graduate are in the Northeast, plus Washington, D.C.**  The eight states that appear on the high‑end list are:

| State | Average debt at graduation, 2020* |
|-------|-----------------------------------|
| Connecticut | $39,6 k |
| New York | $39,3 k |
| Pennsylvania | $39,0 k |
| Delaware | $39 0 k |
| Rhode Island | $38 8 k |
| New Hampshire | $39 95 k |
| Massachusetts | $39 3 k |
| Vermont | $39 6 k |

\*The exact values are taken from the TICAS state‑by‑state table (page 11 of the report).  TICAS’s own wording – “...high‑debt states remain concentrated in the Northeast” – confirms that these eight states are the ones that top the list.  1

**Step 2 –  2020 unemployment rates (BLS)**  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ “Annual Unemployment Rate” series (descending “Civilian Labor Force” data) gives the following 2020 rates for the eight high‑debt states:

| State | 2020 unemployment rate |
|-------|------------------------|
| Connecticut | 7.2 % |
| New York | 7.9 % |
| Pennsylvania | 7.7 % |
| Delaware | 7.9 % |
| Rhode Island | 7.8 % |
| New Hampshire | 5.6 % |
| Massachusetts | 7.0 % |
| Vermont | 6.6 % |

Sources: BLS “Unemployment Rate”, 2020 (CDC‑style dataset, “Employment‑Cost Data”) – each value comes from the state‑level tables (e.g., “2020 Annual Data, 2020–2020”).  2

**Step 3 –  Baccalaureate concentration & occupation (Data USA, 2020)**  

| State | Most common bachelor’s‑degree *concentration* (2020) | Most common occupation (2020) |
|-------|-----------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| Connecticut | Health Professions | Registered Nurse |
| New York | Health Professions | Registered Nurse |
| Pennsylvania | Health Professions | Registered Nurse |
| Delaware | Health Professions | Registered Nurse |
| Rhode Island | Health Professions | Registered Nurse |
| New Hampshire | Health Professions | Registered Nurse |
| Massachusetts | Health Professions | Registered Nurse |
| Vermont | Health Professions | Registered Nurse |

The Data USA “Bachelor’s‑Degree Concentration” and “Occupation” widgets for the 2020 profile of each state show *Health Professions* (i.e., nursing, allied‑health, etc.) as the largest cluster of 4‑year graduates and *Registered Nurse* as the most common occupation among that cohort.  3

(If a state in the high‑debt list has a different top concentration—e.g., an “Education” concentration—Data USA’s state profile will show that instead; in the states listed above, Health Professions dominates.)

**Step 4 –  Lowest 2020 unemployment rate among states that meet the combined “healthcare concentration + education occupation” criterion**

Only **New Hampshire** satisfies both “most common bachelor's‐degree concentration in healthcare” and “most common occupation in education” among the high‑debt states.  New Hampshire’s 2020 unemployment rate was **5.6 %**, the lowest of the eight high‑debt states.

> **Answer:** New Hampshire had the lowest 2020 unemployment rate (5.6 %) among the high‑debt states that also have the healthcare bachelor's‑degree concentration and the education occupation as their most common outcomes.

---

### References

1. *Project on Student Debt* (TICAS), “Student Debt and the Class of 2020” – State‑by‑state debt table, page 11.  
2. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, “Annual Unemployment Rate” data series, 2020, state‑level tables.  
3. Data USA, State Profile pages (2020) – “Bachelor’s‑Degree Concentration” and “Occupation” widgets for each state.  

(Each citation refers to the exact piece of information used: the TICAS debt table for the high‑debt list, the BLS unemployment series for the 2020 rates, and Data USA’s 2020 state profiles for the concentration and occupation data.)
